title: The Land of Light: the Father's heaven in its perfect order
arc: The teaching describes the Land of Light as the celestial state itself — the great land of the Greatness — where every being, tree, and member exists in living conjunction with the Father, summoned from him and established in him, with no admixture of death, falsity, or mingling.
reading:
Although the chapter is heavily damaged, enough survives to show that this is a contemplation of the heavens themselves — the Land of Light considered in its perfection and order, before any descent, any battle, any mingling. The teaching does not narrate a process; it gives a steady description of a state. The opening fixes the subject ("the land of light… in the great land of the Greatness") and then circles around four interlocking features of that state: its substance, its inhabitants, its source, and its order.

First, the substance. The Land of Light is the Father in his outermost expression, the celestial degree itself. Its proper food and medicine are named: "the living ambrosia" and "the living drug." In correspondence these are not two foreign mythological items but two aspects of one reality — the divine good and the divine truth that nourish and heal whatever lives there. They are called "living" because in this state nothing is severed from the Father; every quality is in conjunction with him. The fragment that says of this drug "he too living" makes the point exactly: what the inhabitants take in is not different in kind from what they are. The Land of Light is the state in which receivers and what is received are one life.

Second, the inhabitants. The teaching says "beautiful are the members of their body" and that they live "like all the rich gods" who "were summoned, having come forth from the Father." Read by correspondence, this is the Grand Man at the celestial register: every member, every faculty, every aeon is a particular form of the one Divine Love and Wisdom, and each is "rich" because each is full of what flows in from the Father. They did not arise of themselves; they were called forth, and they remain in the state in which they were called. The "faces" mentioned in the surviving lines are the Faces of Light — the ordered manifestations of Divine Truth, each presenting the inmost in a distinct quality of expression.

Third, the source and the establishing. The teaching repeats that all of this comes "forth from the Father" and that the inhabitants "dwell, being established in him." This is the heart of the description. Heaven is not a place the angels possess; it is a state in which they are continually held by the influx that produced them. The trees, the plants "gushing forth," the gifts of the Greatness — all of these are images of the same one motion: divine good and truth proceeding from the Father and constituting, at every moment, the life of those who receive him. The trees here are perceptions in their celestial form, rooted in the Father and bearing fruit from him; the gushing-forth waters are truth in its living, unmingled flow.

Fourth, the order by negation. The fragment "neither falsehood, neither death, nor [mingling]" defines the Land of Light by what it excludes. It is the opposite state of the cosmos in which the teachings ordinarily place us. There is no falsity-from-evil, no severance from the Lord, and — crucially — no mingled state. What the rest of the corpus describes as the present human condition (the salt sea, the bound Living Soul, the mingling that must be sorted) is simply absent here. This is what makes the Land of Light the pattern and the goal: it is "that which the truth" is, without remainder.

The closing fragments restate the unity of the picture: "the fullness… great light, the living drug… the Greatness; they dwell, being established in him… the gifts of the Great [one]." The whole teaching thus moves, in its small compass, from the naming of the place, to the substance that fills it, to the beings who live by that substance, to the Father from whom both place and beings continually proceed. It is a teaching of pure celestial order — the heavens shown as one continuous emanation in which substance, life, beauty, and dwelling are not four things but one.
